# GitHub parity: every GitHub feature, decided for OSCR

The inventory of what GitHub offers, domain by domain, with a decision for OSCR on each feature: **Reproduce**, **Adapt** or **Exclude**, the night phase that builds it, and its link to research where it has one. It is the reference for `docs/PLATFORM_PLAN.md` (the phases) and for `docs/NIGHT_RUN.md` section 2.1, which asked for it. The storage choice for Git hosting is in `docs/DECISIONS.md` and `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`, not here.

Contents:

1. [Date and method](#1-date-and-method)
2. [Decision rules](#2-decision-rules)
3. [Summary](#3-summary)
4. [Domains of docs.github.com](#4-domains-of-docsgithubcom)
5. [Changelog](#5-changelog)
6. [Addenda from the completeness critics](#6-addenda-from-the-completeness-critics)
7. [Index by night phase](#7-index-by-night-phase)

## 1. Date and method

- **Date**: 2026-09-29, the date of the night run (phase 00 of `docs/NIGHT_RUN.md`). The section files record their reading on 2026-09-27 and 2026-09-28; the latest changelog entry read is dated 2026-09-25.
- **docs.github.com, walked domain by domain.** One researcher per domain (27 domains, section 4), each starting from the domain's entry pages and walking the official documentation page by page, not from memory. A feature is something a user can do or see, settings and options that change behaviour included. Each section lists the pages it read, and each row names its source.
- **The changelog, from 2025-10-01 to 2026-09-29.** Every entry of [github.blog/changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/) in the period, read in full, month by month, in four quarters (section 5): 176 entries (2025-10 to 2025-12), 193 (2026-01 to 2026-03), 260 (2026-04 to 2026-06) and 240 (2026-07 to 2026-09), 869 in all. Every new or changed user-facing feature has a row; a deprecation has one only when it removes a feature; enterprise-only and billing items, and repetitive families (new models, runner images, CodeQL releases), are grouped, one row each.
- **Completeness critics.** Two critics read the inventory's feature names and looked on the web for GitHub features missing under any wording: one through the complete table of contents of docs.github.com and the list of REST API endpoint categories, the other through a researcher's and a maintainer's daily use (every tab and settings page of a repository, a profile and an organization, the `gh` manual, the keyboard shortcuts page). Each feature they found was checked on its documentation page and either skipped (it did not exist, or a row already decided it) or written into an addendum (section 6). The loop stops after two rounds in a row that find nothing, or after four rounds. It ran four rounds (addenda 1.1 and 1.2, 2.1, 3.1, 4.1) and the fourth still found features, so the inventory is as complete as four rounds made it, not proven complete.
- **Assembly.** This file puts the 36 section files of `data/night/parity/` together. Every row is kept as written; the only changes are formatting: headings numbered, a count line under each heading, blank lines where Markdown needed them, and the `<` of placeholders written outside code, such as \<commit> or \<date>, escaped with a backslash, since a renderer would otherwise take them for HTML tags and drop them. No two rows are exact duplicates, so none was merged (section 3.4).
- **Counting.** The section files hold **5,153 feature rows**. The researchers' structured summaries announced 5,158; the tables are the reference, and every table row is in this file.

## 2. Decision rules

| Decision | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Reproduce | OSCR builds the feature, as GitHub offers it, with the research link where it has one (papers by DOI, tracing maps, reproduction reports). |
| Adapt | OSCR builds the feature in another form, and the row says which and why: zero cost, no execution of users' code, no email, in-site notifications only, `science.css` only, or a scientific purpose. |
| Exclude | OSCR does not build it, and the row says why: it is impossible at zero cost, it runs users' code or a generative model on request, it exists only for a paid tier, enterprises or billing, or it is out of scope for research code. |

A decision is taken by applying these criteria **in this order**:

1. zero cost (the free tiers of Cloudflare, D1, Hugging Face and each service; `docs/PLATFORM_PLAN.md` §2);
2. the services' terms of use;
3. security;
4. simplicity;
5. consistency with `CLAUDE.md`.

Standing rules that decide many rows: OSCR never executes users' code, on the Mac or on Cloudflare (`docs/NIGHT_RUN.md` §1, rule 7), so execution features become non-executing checks on OSCR's side or results shown from a GitHub mirror's own CI; no email address is asked for, stored or displayed and notifications stay in the site (`CLAUDE.md`); the only model is the local one on the Mac, between 01:00 and 07:00; a search runs only when its form is submitted; the Worker has 10 ms of CPU per request and 100,000 requests a day, and D1 5 million rows read and 100,000 rows written a day.

The **Phase** column names the night phase of `docs/NIGHT_RUN.md` §3 that builds the feature (01 to 16), or `NEW: <name>` for a proposed new phase, or `-` when nothing is built. When a row names more than one phase, the first is its phase in the counts; the index of section 7 also lists the row under each other phase named outside brackets.

### 3.4 Features found in more than one section

No two rows are identical in every column, so no row was merged: every row of the section files is below, as written. 158 feature names appear in more than one section (330 rows): the domains overlap (a README is both writing and files; limits are both repositories and policy; blocking is both account and moderation), and each section decides the feature from its own angle. Two pairs share the name and the description and differ only in how OSCR builds them; both rows are kept:

- Built-in "Duplicate issue" reply: 01 Writing (Adapt) and 09 Issues (Adapt).
- Push size: 05 Repositories (Adapt) and 25 Site policy, trust and safety (Adapt).

Changelog: https://github.blog/changelog/2024-03-13-authenticate-orcid-id/, 2023-03-02-accessibility-improvements-for-the-contribution-graph, 2025-10-09-improved-blocked-users-view-in-organization-and-personal-settings (via search), 2026-08-21-better-tools-for-managing-blocked-users, 2026-08-27-close-all-open-contributions-authored-by-a-blocked-user (via search), 2026-08-13 / 2026-08-25 / 2026-09-01 block from comments, security advisories and discussion comments (via search), 2026-09-11-profiles-now-show-your-highest-achievement-badge-tier, 2022-04-20 organization profile member-only READMEs (via search). OSCR context: `CLAUDE.md`, `docs/ACCOUNTS.md`, `docs/NIGHT_RUN.md`, `docs/PLATFORM_PLAN.md` §2, `website/src/pages/author/[orcid].astro`.

Decisions taken here (criteria in order: zero cost, the services' terms, security, simplicity, consistency with CLAUDE.md):
- **A user's profile is one static shell plus one Worker request** (`/u/<handle>/` → `GET /api/users/<handle>`), not a static page per account: the static assets hold 20,000 files per version and the catalogue already needs most of them. A verified author's profile and the catalogue's static page `/author/<orcid>/` link to each other.
- **No uploaded pictures**: no free blob store fits personal photos (R2 is not used, KV writes 1,000 a day, D1 is not a blob store, a public Hugging Face dataset would publish personal photos and needs moderation). A generated identicon, or the linked GitHub account's public avatar on request.
- **No email anywhere**, as CLAUDE.md requires: every GitHub email feature is excluded, and attribution goes through an OSCR noreply address built from the account's immutable id, the authenticated pusher, or a linked GitHub account.
- **Achievements become research milestones, in words, without tiers**: no reward for merging without review or for raw counts.
- **A block stops harassment, not scientific criticism**: a blocked or limited user can still send a moderated code-error, code–paper mismatch or reproduction-failure report, and a block never hides a paper's existing reproduction reports.
- **Proposed new phase, "NEW: Account lifecycle"**: handle changes, account deletion with a grace period, data export, successor, account merge, sessions and "sign out everywhere", the settings page, the guide for a change of institution. `docs/ACCOUNTS.md` already lists several of these as not yet built (no deletion, no unlinking, no sign out everywhere).

exist but are undocumented).

Decisions taken here (criteria: zero cost, terms, security, simplicity, CLAUDE.md): (1) every published OSCR release is immutable, with no switch; (2) source archives are built once at publication and stored, never generated on request; (3) OSCR never deposits a release's code on Zenodo (CLAUDE.md: "That code is never redeposited"): an author-requested Zenodo DOI goes on the release's validated tracing map, the code is archived by Software Heritage; (4) the release attestation is signed with an Ed25519 key kept in the Mac's keychain (`org.oscr.release-signing`, to be created by the owner), not with Sigstore; (5) proposed asset caps (50 assets per release, 100 MB per asset, 2 GB of assets per repository), configuration variables to revisit once Phase 00 picks the Git storage.

Decisions taken here (criteria: zero cost, terms, security, simplicity, CLAUDE.md): (1) every write a pull request causes (merge, squash, rebase, "Update branch", a committed suggestion, a conflict resolution, a revert, a fork sync) is an asynchronous merge job doing Git data operations on the Git backend (merge-tree, commit-tree, replay, compare-and-swap of the ref): no working tree, no hooks, no custom merge drivers or filters, never the repository's code; the test merge is computed only when the head or the base moves; (2) checks are OSCR's non-executing checks, commit statuses posted through the API by a lab's own CI, and check runs read from a GitHub mirror, so the merge queue, `merge_group`, `request-checks`, coverage protection and deployments are excluded while auto-merge is kept; (3) stacked pull requests (public preview) are excluded, a pull request can still target another pull request's branch; (4) every Copilot feature is excluded (paid AI); (5) no email anywhere: no email owners in CODEOWNERS, no author email menu, no reply by email; co-authors and merge authors use no-reply addresses and every email in commit metadata is masked (`mask_emails`); (6) pull request pages are dynamic routes (static shell plus JSON), diffs are precomputed per push and loaded per file, and GitHub's diff limits are adopted as configuration so a request fits 10 ms of CPU and the 100,000 daily requests; (7) research: a "Tracing maps" section on every pull request, the verified paper authors first among suggested reviewers, a tracing-map guard that is advisory unless the owner makes it required (an admin can bypass it with a reason when no author has an account), and a merge never alters a validated map (a re-anchoring proposal goes to the author); (8) security: a repository serves only commits reachable from its own refs (no cross-fork SHA access), and push protection has no bypass.

Decisions taken here (criteria: zero cost, terms, security, simplicity, CLAUDE.md):

(1) Projects are rows in the existing D1 database `oscr_community` (no new database, no KV, no Durable Object).

(2) A view loads the whole project once: one Worker request, answered from the Cache API under the project's version number, so D1 is read again only after a change. Filtering, sorting, grouping, slicing, sums and current charts then run in the browser, as you type, at no cost in requests. The rule "a search runs only when the form is submitted" protects the D1 search quota, which a project filter never touches.

(3) Static first: an anonymous reader of a public project gets a static snapshot rebuilt at the nightly deployment ("as of \<date>"). Signed-in members get the live view.

(4) Caps, with one plan for everyone (no Free, Team or Enterprise tiers): 5,000 items per project, archived items included (GitHub: 50,000); 50 fields; 50 options per select field; 5 auto-add workflows; a bulk change of at most 500 items per request. All are configuration variables, to be revisited once measured against D1's 5 M rows read and 100 k rows written a day.

(5) Automations are declarative rules. The Worker evaluates them on the write that changes the item, and the Mac's nightly run evaluates the time-based auto-archive. No GitHub Actions, no Cron Trigger, and no user code runs anywhere.

(6) Notifications from projects (status-update subscriptions, mentions, invitations) stay in the site (D5). Email addresses in any project text are masked (`catalog.mask_emails`), in exports too.

(7) Research: a project can hold papers (by DOI), tracing maps and reproduction reports next to issues, pull requests and drafts. A project can be attached to papers' DOIs, and its roadmap marks the papers' and releases' dates.

(8) Colours and statuses are words. A select option shows its word after a small square swatch (a science.css class), never a pill. A project status says itself with `.ok` / `.warning`.

(9) Historical charts read an append-only log of item changes (one row per change), not daily snapshots.

The September 2026 changelog month page was checked: no other Discussions entry.

Decisions taken here (criteria: zero cost, terms, security, simplicity, CLAUDE.md): (1) discussions live in D1 `oscr_community` (the planned `discussions` and `comments` tables, plus votes, poll votes and edits), written by the Worker, Markdown sanitized at write, never email (D5); (2) besides repositories and organizations, **every paper has a discussion space keyed by its DOI** (the Discussion section the paper page already reserves), where the paper's verified authors hold the maintain role; (3) organization discussions keep GitHub's source-repository model (it reuses repository permissions: simpler than a new scope); (4) no gradients, patterns or emoji badges: pins, states and answers are said in words (`science.css`); (5) poll voters are never shown, one vote per account, options frozen at the first vote; (6) no public "most helpful" leaderboard (gaming), consistent with the achievements decision of `02-account.md`; (7) a hide, a block or a report stops harassment, never scientific criticism: a hide by an author of the criticized paper or code is logged and reversible by OSCR's moderators; (8) one number sequence per repository for issues, pull requests and discussions, so `#123` is never ambiguous; (9) a discussion cited by a reproduction report, an issue or a tracing-map note is closed and locked, not deleted, outside moderation.

the full list of hide reasons comes from a search summary citing [managing-disruptive-comments](https://docs.github.com/en/communities/moderating-comments-and-conversations/managing-disruptive-comments) and [cli/cli#8409](https://github.com/cli/cli/issues/8409) (the GraphQL enum page could not be read: it is now an index).

Decisions taken here (criteria in order: zero cost, the services' terms, security, simplicity, consistency with CLAUDE.md):
- **Two levels of moderation, one queue model.** A repository's own moderation (its admins, writers, and a lab's moderators) and OSCR's (the owner and the platform moderators of Phase 16). Every "Report" offers both; the platform level extends Phase 6's removal requests (`reports`, `oscr reports`), so no new mechanism is needed.
- **Moderation stops harassment, never scientific criticism** (the rule the account inventory set for blocking, extended here to every tool): hiding, locking, deleting, interaction limits, pull request limits and blocks never remove a code-error, code–paper mismatch or reproduction-failure report from the paper's record. A hidden report stays listed and counted on the paper's page with its reason in words; only OSCR's moderators can remove one, for abuse, and the removal is logged.
- **No email anywhere in this domain** (CLAUDE.md): community health files are rendered with every address masked (`catalog.mask_emails`); the code-of-conduct templates' "contact" field becomes the address of the repository's in-site report form; a `mailto:` contact link is refused; reports ask for no email and are answered in the site; a blocked person's notification is an in-site notification.
- **Community health files are read, never run**: plain text read at each push of the default branch (a size cap per file), the result stored as one facts row per repository in D1, so a repository page needs no Git read. The community profile gains research items (a linked paper DOI, `CITATION.cff`, an environment file, a data availability statement, a tracing map) said in words; the API keeps GitHub's `health_percentage` for compatibility, computed on GitHub's items only.
- **The wiki is a second Git repository** (`<repo>.wiki.git`) in the same `GitBackend` as the code, behind the same tokens and push gate (secret detection, size limits, known-malware check), rendered by the shared Markdown and reStructuredText renderer. Opening its editing to "everyone" means any signed-in OSCR account, behind Turnstile, with blocks and interaction limits applied, and the pages stay `noindex` while it is open.
- **Expiries are compared when read** (interaction limits, temporary blocks): no cron, no D1 write when a limit ends.
- **Deletion hides; redaction erases.** A deleted comment leaves the public outputs and stays on the Mac as the moderation record; "Delete revision from history" (a leaked secret or personal data) erases the revision's text everywhere, the Mac's copy included, keeping only who and when.

polled by the Mac, no email), `oscr/repofeatures.py` (environment files, detected tools), `oscr/repos.py` (`license_of`, SPDX), `oscr/scriptstore.py`.

Decisions taken here (criteria in order: zero cost, the services' terms, security, simplicity, CLAUDE.md):
1. **Vulnerability data comes from OSV.** The Mac downloads OSV's per-ecosystem archives every night (free, no key, no stated rate limit; PyPI, CRAN, Bioconductor, Julia, npm, crates.io, Go, Maven and more) and matches them against every repository's dependency graph. Matching only parses text. Each record keeps its source and license, for example GitHub's and PyPA's data under CC BY 4.0, and the alert page shows the attribution.
2. **Secret detection uses regular expressions and nothing else.** OSCR vendors an open rule set (gitleaks' rules, MIT) and adds its own rules for research services. There are no validity checks and no partner notifications: OSCR never sends a user's credential to anyone. When a secret is found, the push is refused. The only accepted bypass reasons are "false positive" and "used in tests". "I'll fix it later" is refused on public repositories, because it would publish a live credential. A push that cannot be scanned completely is refused, never skipped.
3. **OSCR runs no code.** It does not run CodeQL, does not submit dependencies automatically by resolving builds, does not run a package resolver and does not vendor dependencies. The CodeQL terms also forbid hosting CodeQL as a service without a paid licence. Code scanning therefore means SARIF files uploaded by external CI. The usual source is the GitHub mirror's Actions, where CodeQL is free for open-source code hosted on GitHub.com. OSCR stores and shows those results.
4. **Alerts are private to maintainers**, as on GitHub, which "never publicly discloses insecure dependencies". The public sees the security policy and published advisories only.
5. **Update pull requests are off by default and opt-in.** A paper's pinned environment is part of its reproducibility. When turned on, OSCR only edits manifest pins as text and never touches a release tied to a paper. In GitHub mirror mode OSCR leaves updates to the mirror's Dependabot and shows its pull requests, instead of duplicating them.
6. **Private vulnerability reporting is on by default** for OSCR-hosted public repositories. Reporting requires sign-in and Turnstile, and notifications stay in the site only.
7. **OSCR is not a CVE Numbering Authority.** A maintainer can enter an existing CVE. OSCR-published advisories go into the open data as OSV JSON. The same machinery also carries *scientific* advisories: code errors that affect published results.
8. **No AI feature and no email.** That leaves out Autofix, AI Scan, AI-detected secrets, the AI regex generator and assignment to agents, and all notifications stay in the site.

jobs), `data/night/storage/cloudflare-capacity.md` (the Worker's share of D1 writes: 10,000 rows a day).

Decisions taken here (criteria: zero cost, the services' terms, security, simplicity, CLAUDE.md): (1) **OSCR executes nothing a user deposits, anywhere** (not on the Mac, not on Cloudflare): workflows, runners, marketplace actions, caches, artifacts, secrets, variables and environments are excluded as execution features. (2) GitHub's "Actions" tab becomes a **Checks tab** with three sources of results: *OSCR checks*, a fixed catalogue of non-executing checks written in the `oscr` package, run by the Mac's job runner after each push, that read the pushed tree as data and never import or run it; *CI (mirror)*, the check runs, commit statuses and workflow runs of the linked GitHub (or GitLab) repository, read by the Mac with the existing read-only token `org.oscr.github`; *integrations and people*, through OSCR's Commit statuses and Checks APIs. (3) An outside CI can post results without any stored secret: **OSCR accepts GitHub Actions OIDC tokens** (it is the relying party, not the issuer). The Worker checks the RS256 signature against GitHub's published keys (cached), the issuer, the audience (the site's URL) and that `repository_id` is the one linked to the OSCR repository; otherwise a personal token with the `statuses:write` scope (Phase 09). No new secret for the owner to create. (4) Only OSCR itself and integrations the owner registers create **check runs**, because they carry Markdown and line annotations shown inside code views. Anyone with a scoped token posts **commit statuses**. (5) Limits sized for the Worker's 10,000 D1 rows written a day: 100 statuses per commit and context, 50 check runs per suite, 50 annotations per request and 200 per check run, 64 KiB per output field; when the day's write budget is spent, the API answers 429 with a clear message. (6) **Retention**: results on a commit pinned by a release, a tracing map or a paper's cited commit are kept for good, as provenance; other results leave D1 after 400 days and stay on the Mac. (7) The mirror's **logs and artifacts stay on GitHub**, behind a link. They are never copied, because of storage and because a log can contain anything. (8) The **status badge** is a Worker route with one D1 read and `Cache-Control: max-age=3600`, not one static file per repository (the static-file cap is 20,000). (9) OSCR checks on **pull requests from forks run without approval**: they execute nothing, and there is no token or secret to leak. (10) The GitHub Actions templates OSCR documents for mirrors only test the researcher's own project, as GitHub's Actions terms require ("production, testing, deployment, or publication of the software project"), on GitHub's free standard runners for public repositories.

free, needs no account, public repositories only, capped memory, no GPU, no persistent storage; it builds from requirements.txt, environment.yml or a Dockerfile).

Decisions taken here (criteria in order: zero cost, the services' terms, security, simplicity, CLAUDE.md):
1. **OSCR hosts no package registry and no container image.** A registry would cost storage and bandwidth beyond the free tiers. Every client request (npm, Maven, NuGet, gem, docker) would also use up the Worker's 100,000 daily requests. And a registry distributes executables that OSCR cannot vet. Researchers already publish to free public registries (PyPI, CRAN, Bioconductor, conda-forge, npm, Maven Central, NuGet, RubyGems, Docker Hub, ghcr.io). OSCR instead records those packages and images as **package records**. Each record is pinned by version or by digest, checked against the registry from the Mac (read-only metadata, never a download or an install), and tied to releases (07), tracing maps and papers.
2. **OSCR hosts no user website.** Pages becomes the **Docs view**. It renders the repository's Markdown (root or `docs/`) in the browser, at a chosen commit, with the same sanitized renderer as the README (phase 02) and `science.css`. The author's HTML, CSS and JavaScript never run on OSCR's origin. There are no builds (Jekyll/Liquid would mean executing the author's templates), no themes and no custom domains.
3. **OSCR runs no development environment**: nothing on the Mac and nothing on Cloudflare. Codespaces become an **Environment panel**. It reads `devcontainer.json`, the Dockerfile and environment files (`requirements.txt`, `environment.yml`, `renv.lock`, `Project.toml`…) as text. It adds **"Run on your machine" instructions** and **"Open elsewhere" links** to services that visitors use under their own accounts and quotas: GitHub Codespaces for a GitHub mirror, and Binder for a public repository. OSCR never runs a lifecycle command, never stores a user secret and never forwards a port.
4. **One new phase is proposed, "NEW: Environments and packages"**, for the package records, the container pins, the Environment panel and the Open-elsewhere links. It builds on phases 01 (storage), 02 (rendering) and 07 (releases). Everything else in this domain goes to phases 01–16.
5. **The paper's commit comes first.** The Docs view, the Environment panel and the Open-elsewhere links default to the commit or tag that a validated tracing map or a paper's release cites, and fall back to the default branch.

| Feature | What it does | Decision | In OSCR (how, or why not) | Phase | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hosted package registries (GitHub Packages as a service) | Host software packages privately or publicly next to the code, to use as dependencies in other projects | Exclude | Decision 1: storage and bandwidth beyond free tiers, the Worker's daily request quota spent by package clients, and executables OSCR cannot vet. Public registries already do this for free. OSCR records packages published elsewhere instead (next rows) | NEW: Environments and packages | pk-intro, pk-billing |
| Supported ecosystems and clients | npm (`package.json`), RubyGems (`Gemfile`, `gem`), Maven (`pom.xml`), Gradle (`build.gradle`), NuGet (`nupkg`, `dotnet`), Docker/OCI containers | Adapt | The Mac detects packages from manifest files at each synced commit, as text and never executed. Covered: those six plus the science ecosystems (`pyproject.toml`/`setup.cfg` → PyPI, `DESCRIPTION` → CRAN/Bioconductor, `meta.yaml`/`environment.yml` → conda-forge, `Project.toml` → Julia General). Each detected name becomes a proposed package record that a repository writer confirms | NEW: Environments and packages | pk-intro |
| Push a container image to ghcr.io | `docker push ghcr.io/NAMESPACE/IMAGE:TAG`, authenticated with a PAT (classic) or `GITHUB_TOKEN` | Exclude | No image hosting (decision 1). An image stays on Docker Hub, ghcr.io or quay.io | NEW: Environments and packages | pk-container |
| Pull an image by tag or by digest | `docker pull …:1.14.1` or `docker pull …@sha256:…` | Adapt | A container record stores the reference **pinned by digest**, with the tag kept only as a label. Decisions taken here (criteria in order: zero cost, the services' terms, security, simplicity, CLAUDE.md):
1. **No generative model runs on request, anywhere.** Not GitHub's, not a provider's, and not Cloudflare Workers AI: its free plan gives 10,000 neurons a day and then fails with an error ("Upgrade to Workers Paid"), far too little for a public site, and it would put a hosted model between readers and the authors' code. Every chat, completion, summary-by-model and model-picker feature is therefore excluded. This is consistent with the earlier sections (06, 09, 11, 13, 14).
2. **No coding agent.** Copilot's cloud agent, code review agent, CLI, app and agentic workflows build, test and run code. OSCR never executes users' code, on the Mac or on Cloudflare (NIGHT_RUN §1 rule 7), so every agent feature is excluded, with its settings, firewall, environment, secrets, memory and integrations.
3. **The only model is the local one on the Mac, from 01:00 to 07:00** (CLAUDE.md). It reads text, works in batches, and never touches a repository's code to run it. What it produces is a suggestion labelled "set by the model" with its confidence, and a person accepts it. Rules come first, as in 09 (triage suggestions) and 05 ("Similar issues").
4. **OSCR takes the purpose of a feature, never its model.** A pull request's "change summary" is computed from the diff and the tracing maps. "Code referencing" becomes "identical copies", found by the SHA-256 digests OSCR already stores. Spaces become Collections of papers, files and line ranges at a commit. The GitHub MCP server becomes `oscr mcp`: a read-only server inside the `oscr` command-line tool. It runs on the researcher's machine, for the researcher's own assistant, so OSCR hosts no model and pays nothing. Prompt files (`.prompt.yml`, `.prompt.md`) are displayed as structured documents that a tracing map can point to, because papers that use a language model publish their prompts as part of their Methods.
5. **Retired products are listed and excluded:** GitHub Models (retired on 2026-07-30: playground, catalogue, inference API and BYOK), Spark, Copilot Extensions (2025-11-10), knowledge bases and the `gh-copilot` extension.
6. **AI training.** The hosting terms say that OSCR trains no model on hosted code and gives hosted code to no one for training. A repository setting, off by default because the license governs reuse, asks known AI-training crawlers not to use the repository through `robots.txt`. The page says plainly that this is a request, not a lock.
7. **New phase proposed: "Automated-decision transparency".** It covers the "about automated decisions" page, the "set by rule, model or person" label with its confidence, and the corrections of automated values. It takes over what Copilot's responsible-use notes and thumbs-up or thumbs-down feedback do.

Decisions taken here (criteria in order: zero cost, the services' terms, security, simplicity, CLAUDE.md): (1) an OSCR organization is a **lab** (a lab, research group, consortium, institute, core facility or software collaboration), free, with every GitHub Team or Enterprise Cloud organization feature that costs nothing to run (custom roles, rulesets, announcement banner, audit log API, access export), and no billing, seat, plan, enterprise, identity-provider or Actions feature; (2) validating a tracing map for a Zenodo DOI is **never** a role: whatever their lab or repository role, only a verified author of the paper (ORCID) validates (CLAUDE.md, "DOIs and Zenodo"); (3) invitations, requests, reminders and 2FA notices are **in-site notifications** only (D5), and people are invited by OSCR handle, ORCID iD or GitHub login, never by email; (4) no IP address, country or email is stored or shown, so the audit log has no location qualifier; (5) the "2FA requirement" is the passkey requirement already chosen for authentication (04 section), and non-compliant people lose write access rather than being removed; (6) D1 writes are scarce (100,000 a day, shared): the audit log keeps 180 days, clones and fetches are not logged, API insights are one counter row per day, custom roles are capped at 10 per lab and team nesting at 5 levels; (7) deleting a parent team moves its child teams up one level instead of deleting them; (8) renaming a lab keeps permanent redirects and reserves the old handle, because DOI metadata and papers cite repository URLs and map permalinks; (9) a lab's members-only README is a size-capped setting stored in D1, not a private repository, because OSCR repositories are private only while embargoed.

refresh for OAuth apps). Outside GitHub, for the decisions: developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits (Free plan: 100,000 requests a day, 10 ms CPU per request and per Cron Trigger, 50 subrequests, `waitUntil` up to 30 s, Cron Trigger wall time 15 min, 5 Cron Triggers), developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/bindings/rate-limit and its GA changelog of 2025-09-19 (10 or 60 s windows, counted per location, eventually consistent; whether the Free plan includes it is not stated: to check at build time).

**The decisions taken for this domain** (criteria in order: zero cost, the services' terms, security, simplicity, consistency with `CLAUDE.md`):

1. **One public REST API, no GraphQL.** OSCR has `/api/forge/v1/` on the Worker it already runs, described by an OpenAPI 3.1 file. GraphQL is excluded for now: a nested query must fit in 10 ms of CPU and 50 D1 queries, and a single query could spend much of the 5 M rows D1 lets OSCR read each day. Guarding that with a query-cost system would add a lot of machinery. REST resources that bundle related records (a paper with its repositories and maps) and the open-data dumps cover the "everything in one call" need.
2. **Small quotas within the Worker's 100,000 requests a day.** Every dynamic route shares that allowance: the site's search, sign-in and the API. The API gets quotas far below GitHub's and its own share of the day. Once that share is spent, it answers with a 429 that says the reason in words and gives `Retry-After` up to 00:00 UTC, as `website/worker/api.ts` already does for D1's quota. Reads that a static page or a static JSON file can carry stay static, since static requests are free and unlimited.
3. **Webhooks are sent by the Worker, never by the Mac.** Events go into a D1 outbox: the Worker writes them for actions taken on the site, and the Mac's D1 push writes them for Git events. A Cron Trigger every 5 minutes uses 1 of the 5 free ones. Each run sends about 40 deliveries (the Free plan allows 50 subrequests per invocation), within a daily budget. Deliveries therefore take up to 5 minutes, not a few seconds. The Mac never sends a request to an address a user typed: that would open the home network to server-side request forgery. The Mac still listens to nothing.
4. **Webhook secrets are stored encrypted.** An HMAC-SHA256 signature needs the secret in clear when signing, so it cannot be stored as a hash. Secrets are encrypted with AES-GCM in D1, under a key kept as a Cloudflare secret. **Secret for the owner to create: `WEBHOOK_KEY`** (32 random bytes).
5. **One kind of integration.** An "OSCR application" does what GitHub splits between GitHub Apps and OAuth apps: a user authorizes it with OAuth 2.0 (authorization code with PKCE, or the device flow), and it can optionally be installed on an account or organization for selected repositories. It gets fine-grained permissions only, tokens that expire, and one webhook. OSCR stores only the application's public keys: the developer generates the key pair and OSCR never holds a private key.
6. **The Marketplace keeps no commerce.** No paid plans, trials, purchases or payouts (zero cost). What remains is a free, moderated "Integrations" directory of public OSCR applications, grouped by research use.
7. **Mirror mode receives GitHub's events without the Mac listening.** A GitHub App, registered by the owner, sends its webhooks to a Worker route. The route checks `X-Hub-Signature-256` against a Cloudflare secret and writes one job row, which the Mac polls. Without that App, the Mac polls GitHub each night with conditional requests (a 304 does not count against GitHub's rate limit). **Secret for the owner to create if the App is registered: `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET`.**

Decisions taken here (criteria in order: zero cost, the services' terms, security, simplicity, CLAUDE.md), consistent with the sections already written (`04-authentication.md`, `05-repos-manage.md`, `07-releases.md`, `13-code-security.md`, `14-actions.md`, `15-packages-pages-codespaces.md`, `17-search.md`): (1) **no native desktop or mobile app**: publishing on the App Store needs Apple's paid Developer Program (99 USD a year) and signed macOS and Windows apps need paid certificates, so zero cost excludes them; the site is built for phones (phase 15) and can be added to a home screen with a web app manifest, and every Git client, GitHub Desktop included, works against OSCR over HTTPS (phase 01); (2) the `oscr` command-line tool keeps its token **only in the system keychain**: no plain-text fallback (`--insecure-storage` is not reproduced), `OSCR_TOKEN` for headless use; (3) `oscr` sends **no telemetry** and asks the server nothing it does not need; (4) the API is **REST only**, no GraphQL; (5) **no extension installer**: `oscr` runs `oscr-<name>` programs found on the `PATH`, as Git does, and never downloads executables for users; (6) **no AI features** (Copilot Chat, agents, commit-message or conflict generation): paid models, code sent to third parties, and the Mac's GPU is reserved to classification between 01:00 and 07:00; (7) `oscr` **neutralizes terminal escape sequences** in repository content and comments by default; (8) nothing that stores users' CI secrets or runs their code (secrets, variables, caches, artifacts, codespaces), as decided in `14-actions.md`.

| `gh help reference` and the online manual with examples | One page listing every command and flag; a page of usage examples | Reproduce | `oscr help reference` and a generated reference page on the site, with worked research examples (link a paper, propose a tracing map, cite a repository) | 14 | man:gh_help_reference, examples, cli-reference |
| Built-in short forms | `ls`, `new`, `co`, `rm`, `cs`, `rs`, `at`, `ext` aliases of commands | Reproduce | `ls`, `new`, `co` and `rm` where the command exists | 14 | man:gh_repo_list, man:gh_pr_checkout |
| Repository selection | `-R/--repo [HOST/]OWNER/REPO` on targeted commands; otherwise the repository of the current clone | Reproduce | Same, inferred from the OSCR remote of the clone; research: in a clone that has both a GitHub `origin` and an OSCR mirror remote, OSCR's is chosen | 14 | man:gh_pr, man:gh_repo_set-default |
| `gh repo set-default` | Chooses the default remote repository of a clone with several remotes (`--view`, `--unset`) | Reproduce | `oscr repo set-default`, stored in the clone's own Git configuration | 14 | man:gh_repo_set-default |
| `GH_REPO` | Environment variable naming the repository for commands run outside a clone | Reproduce | `OSCR_REPO` | 14 | man:gh_help_environment |

| Editor mode | `-e/--editor` writes title and body in a text editor (first line is the title); `prefer_editor_prompt`; `GH_EDITOR`, `GIT_EDITOR`, `VISUAL`, `EDITOR` | Reproduce | Same flag, setting and variables (`OSCR_EDITOR` first) | 14 | man:gh_issue_create, man:gh_config, man:gh_help_environment |

### 4.21 Gists: public and secret gists, revisions, forks, stars, comments, embedding, cloning, several files, rendering

*File `data/night/parity/21-gists.md`: 99 rows (Reproduce 58, Adapt 35, Exclude 6).*

Sources read (2026-09-28): [hub](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/writing-on-github/editing-and-sharing-content-with-gists) ; [create](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/writing-on-github/editing-and-sharing-content-with-gists/creating-gists) ; [fork](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/writing-on-github/editing-and-sharing-content-with-gists/forking-and-cloning-gists) ; [star](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/writing-on-github/editing-and-sharing-content-with-gists/saving-gists-with-stars) ; [moderate](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/writing-on-github/editing-and-sharing-content-with-gists/moderating-gist-comments) ; [ghes](https://docs.github.com/en/enterprise-server@3.17/get-started/writing-on-github/editing-and-sharing-content-with-gists/creating-gists) ; [about-old](https://docs.github.com/en/enterprise/2.13/user/articles/about-gists) ; [rest](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/gists/gists) ; [rest-comments](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/gists/comments) ; [graphql](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/gists) ; [search](https://docs.github.com/en/search-github/searching-on-github/searching-gists) ; [pin](https://docs.github.com/en/account-and-profile/how-tos/profile-customization/pinning-items-to-your-profile) ; [partners](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/concepts/secret-security/secret-scanning-for-partners) ; [emu](https://docs.github.com/en/enterprise-cloud@latest/admin/managing-iam/understanding-iam-for-enterprises/abilities-and-restrictions-of-managed-user-accounts) ; [scopes](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/oauth-apps/building-oauth-apps/scopes-for-oauth-apps) ; [fgpat](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/authentication/permissions-required-for-fine-grained-personal-access-tokens) ; [username](https://docs.github.com/en/account-and-profile/concepts/username-changes) ; [malware](https://docs.github.com/en/site-policy/acceptable-use-policies/github-active-malware-or-exploits) ; [non-code](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/working-with-files/using-files/working-with-non-code-files) ; [events](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/github-event-types) (no gist event type) ; [report](https://docs.github.com/en/communities/maintaining-your-safety-on-github/reporting-abuse-or-spam) and [blocking](https://docs.github.com/en/communities/maintaining-your-safety-on-github/blocking-a-user-from-your-personal-account) (neither mentions gists) ; [changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/?label=gists) (no gist entry in the last twelve months) ; GitHub CLI [cli-gist](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_gist), [cli-create](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_gist_create), [cli-list](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_gist_list), [cli-edit](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_gist_edit), [cli-view](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_gist_view), [cli-rename](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_gist_rename), [cli-delete](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_gist_delete), [cli-clone](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_gist_clone) ; GitHub community answer [cd-62203](https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/62203) (directories refused at push) ; public gist pages observed signed out: [ui-discover](https://gist.github.com/discover), [ui-user](https://gist.github.com/octocat), [ui-gist](https://gist.github.com/octocat/9257657), [ui-revisions](https://gist.github.com/octocat/9257657/revisions), [ui-embed](https://gist.github.com/octocat/9257657.js), [ui-md](https://gist.github.com/yashika51/58d2b6d8d1048a1d0a9ea5949a8aa7f6), [ui-nb](https://gist.github.com/fperez/9716279).

Decisions taken for this domain (criteria: zero cost, terms, security, simplicity, CLAUDE.md): an OSCR gist is a **snippet** (phase 13); each snippet is a small Git repository on the phase 01 `GitBackend` (so clone, push, fork and revisions reuse phase 01 and 02), and its metadata (description, visibility, paper anchors, stars, comments, subscriptions) are rows in D1 `oscr_community`. "Secret" is said "unlisted" (random 128-bit id, never indexed), because a secret gist is not private. HTTPS only, no SSH (a Worker cannot accept SSH). Embeds are iframes of a static page, never a third-party script. A snippet gets **no Zenodo DOI** (CLAUDE.md reserves DOIs for tracing maps validated by an author); it is cited by its permanent revision URL. Limits: 100 files and 10 MB per snippet, 1 MB shown inline per file (a larger set belongs in a repository).

[lists-limit](https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/113251) (the 32-list limit, stated by GitHub staff in community discussions), [achievements-list](https://github.com/Schweinepriester/github-profile-achievements) (a community list of the achievements and their thresholds; GitHub's docs do not list them). Watching is inventoried in full in `03-notifications.md`, the profile in `02-account.md`, topics on a repository in `06-repos-files.md`; the rows here that touch them keep the same decisions.

Decisions taken here (criteria in order: zero cost, the services' terms, security, simplicity, CLAUDE.md): (1) the social rows live in D1 `oscr_community`: a `stars` table (account, target kind, target id, date; unique), a `follows` table for people and organizations, star lists on the planned `collections` and `collection_items` tables, the planned `subscriptions` for catalogue entities (authors by ORCID iD, journals, tools, datasets, categories), and the feed read from the `events` rows that notifications already write (03); every write is one Worker request behind the session check, under per-account daily caps (the 100,000 writes a day). (2) Explore, trending, topic pages and curated collections are static pages rebuilt nightly by the Mac from the day's rows (it already pulls community rows with `oscr community`), with a bounded file count under the 20,000-file limit. (3) Featured topics and curated collections are Markdown files in a public `explore` repository hosted on OSCR, in github/explore's format, reviewed by pull request, checked by non-executing lint (Phase 10), content CC BY 4.0. (4) Ranking is research-first: confirmed reproductions, validated tracing maps and papers that use the code come before stars; no badges with tiers, no leaderboards of raw counts. (5) No money moves through OSCR: GitHub Sponsors is excluded entirely; `FUNDING.yml` becomes a "Funding" box of plain links plus the grants of the linked papers. (6) Privacy: stargazer and watcher lists only for maintainers, follower lists only for signed-in viewers, personalized recommendations computed in the viewer's browser, private profiles kept out of feeds and trending. (7) No email: the Explore newsletter becomes Atom feeds and an opt-in digest in the site's inbox.

### 4.23 Repository insights: pulse, contributors, community standards, commit activity, code frequency, dependency graph and dependents ("used by"), network graph, forks list, traffic (views, clones, referrers, popular content)

*File `data/night/parity/23-insights.md`: 72 rows (Reproduce 44, Adapt 22, Exclude 6).*

for OSCR's traffic source: Cloudflare Web Analytics [cf-wa-about](https://developers.cloudflare.com/web-analytics/about/), [cf-wa-metrics](https://developers.cloudflare.com/web-analytics/data-metrics/high-level-metrics/), [cf-wa-faq](https://developers.cloudflare.com/web-analytics/faq/), [cf-graphql](https://developers.cloudflare.com/analytics/graphql-api/) (search summary); OSCR: `docs/NIGHT_RUN.md` (phase 12), `docs/PLATFORM_PLAN.md` §2 (Workers 100,000 requests a day and 10 ms CPU, D1 100 k rows written a day, static requests free), `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` (a signed-out page view asks the Worker nothing), and, for consistency, the sections 02 (account), 07 (releases), 11 (discussions), 12 (communities), 13 (code security) and 14 (actions) of `data/night/parity/`.

Decisions taken here (criteria in order: zero cost, the services' terms, security, simplicity, CLAUDE.md):
1. **Insights are computed by the Mac, never on request.** The Mac reads each repository's Git history as data (`git log --numstat` on a bare copy; no code of the repository is run), incrementally, commit by commit, and writes one insights row per repository to D1 (contributors, weekly commits, additions and deletions, network layout, forks), rewritten only when the repository changed. One static shell page serves every repository's insights with one Worker request, so the file budget of the static site is not spent per repository. As a result there is no 10,000-commit limit, and the API answers `202` only while a job is queued.
2. **Page views come from Cloudflare Web Analytics**: free, with no cookie, no client-side state and no personal data collected (Cloudflare's statement). Its beacon goes to `cloudflareinsights.com`, never to the Worker, so a signed-out reader's page view still costs no Worker request. Each night, within the 7-day window in which Cloudflare keeps the data unsampled, the Mac reads the previous day's page views and visits per path and per referring host through Cloudflare's GraphQL Analytics API. It uses a read-only analytics token that the owner creates (keychain `org.oscr.cloudflare-analytics`, to note under "À valider par Yann"). The Content Security Policy gains `static.cloudflareinsights.com` (script) and `cloudflareinsights.com` (connect). **To verify before phase 12**: that the free plan's GraphQL API exposes the Web Analytics dataset. If it does not, traffic shows clones and downloads only, and the gap is reported. This source also makes page views possible for discussions insights (section 11 left them out for lack of a source).
3. **No per-person tracking.** Unique visitors and unique cloners are left out, because they need an identifier per person (an IP address, a cookie or an account). Cloudflare's "visits" take their place: page views that came from another site or a direct link. Referrers are kept as a host only, with no path and no query. No IP address is stored. Traffic is private to maintainers (write role), as on GitHub.
4. **Clones are counted at OSCR's Git front** (phase 01): an upload-pack request with no `have` line is a full clone, and each one is one D1 upsert per repository per UTC day. In GitHub mirror mode, clones made on GitHub are not counted. GitHub's traffic API needs the "Administration: read" permission, and OSCR's GitHub App keeps to least privilege, so the page links to GitHub's own traffic page instead.
5. **Contributors are identified without email**, as decided in the account section: by the OSCR noreply address, by the authenticated pusher, or by a linked GitHub login in mirror mode. Any other author is shown by the name written in the commit, with `.mailmap` applied and emails masked (`catalog.mask_emails`).
6. **Research overlay.** The time charts mark the linked papers' dates (preprint, publication, correction) and the releases tied to paper versions, so a reader sees whether the code changed after publication. The network graph and the activity view mark the commits that a paper or a tracing map cites.
7. **Charts are SVG styled by `science.css` classes**, each with a real `table` twin. Status is said in words and never shown by colour alone. CSV, PNG and SVG files are made in the browser (zero cost).

blog [blog-a11y](https://github.blog/open-source/building-githubs-next-chapter-in-accessibility/), [blog-tree](https://github.blog/engineering/user-experience/considerations-for-making-a-tree-view-component-accessible/), [blog-codeview](https://github.blog/engineering/user-experience/accessibility-considerations-behind-code-search-and-code-view/), [blog-codeview2](https://github.blog/2023-06-21-crafting-a-better-faster-code-view) ; OSCR's own `science.css` and `Base.astro` (contrast measured here).

Decisions taken for this domain (criteria in order: zero cost, the services' terms, security, simplicity, CLAUDE.md): (1) **Display and accessibility preferences** live in the browser (localStorage, wrapped in try/catch) for everyone, signed in or not, on one static page `/settings/display/`; a signed-in account also keeps them in its `oscr_community` row, delivered by the `/api/account/me` answer the page already asks for: no extra Worker request per page view. A few lines of inline script in `Base.astro` set `data-*` attributes on `<html>` before the first paint; `science.css` holds every rule keyed on those attributes (no `style` attribute, no utility class, no other CSS file). (2) **Light stays the default** (CLAUDE.md: no dark theme by default); dark, "follow the system", increased contrast and the colour-blind-safe palette are opt-in. (3) **The command palette and the file finder filter only data already in the browser** (commands, the page's links, recently visited pages, one static and immutable file list per commit); anything that needs the D1 search runs **only on Enter**, never as you type (CLAUDE.md search rule, and the Workers limit of 100,000 dynamic requests a day). (4) **No native mobile app** (Apple Developer Program at $99 a year, store reviews, a second codebase): the site is responsive and installable through a web app manifest, **without push notifications** (D5: notifications in the site only). (5) **GitHub's keys are kept**, so researchers coming from GitHub keep their habits; OSCR adds research keys only on free letters. (6) **Target WCAG 2.2 AA**, checked with axe-core (MPL-2.0, free) against the built static pages, plus keyboard, VoiceOver and NVDA checks; an accessibility statement lists the known gaps in words. Two gaps measured today in `science.css`: the focus ring `#e8a200` has 2.19:1 against white (WCAG 1.4.11 asks 3:1), and link blue `#0645ad` has 2.46:1 against the black text (links in running text need an underline, WCAG 1.4.1).

Decisions taken for this domain (criteria in order: zero cost, the services' terms, security, simplicity, CLAUDE.md):

(1) **An import is a Mac job that fetches a public source as data** (no checkout, hooks off, no submodule recursion, LFS smudge off, `transfer.fsckObjects` on, a byte counter that stops at the quota), requested through a D1 `jobs` row the Mac polls (nothing on the Mac listens). It **keeps every Git object byte for byte**, so commit hashes are the source's: the commit a paper cites, the tracing maps (lines at a commit) and the SWHIDs resolve unchanged. OSCR never rewrites an imported history.

(2) **Who may import**: the verified owner of the source (GitHub sign-in plus the `repo_owner` fact), or a verified author of a paper linked to it (`paper_orcid`), or anyone when the repository's license allows redistribution **and** is confirmed by its own license file (for an archive without one: by its record), the same rule as the scripts store. Otherwise the import is refused and the page keeps linking to the source.

(3) **Only code and the owner's own metadata are copied** (description, topics, homepage, license, releases and their assets, labels and milestones, the wiki). Issues, pull or merge requests, discussions, reviews and comments written by other people are **linked, not copied**: GitHub's and GitLab's terms license that content for display on their service, and the commenters never agreed to OSCR.

(4) **No third-party credentials**: OSCR asks for no token or password of another service; a private source is pushed by its owner from their own machine.

(5) **Email addresses**: imported commits keep their bytes (decision 1); every OSCR view masks addresses (`catalog.mask_emails`), and Git clients receive the objects as the public source serves them. New pushes go through the no-reply gate of phases 03 and 11, so a mirror push of a history carrying addresses is refused and the message points to the import.

(6) **Attribution without email**: OSCR stores no email address, so a commit is matched to an account through GitHub's public commit-author login when the account has linked that GitHub identity; any other commit author is a placeholder identity that the owner can reattribute, and the person must accept.

(7) **Archiving**: every public OSCR repository is sent to Software Heritage (Save Code Now) at creation or import, at each release, and after pushes at most once an hour per repository, within the shared budget of 120 requests an hour without a token. SWHIDs of files, directories and commits are computed locally from the Git ids, so every line permalink also has a SWHID.

(8) **Exports are assembled in the reader's browser or by the `oscr` tool from paginated API pages** (the Worker has 10 ms of CPU): nothing is stored on the server, no link expires, nothing is sent by email.

Keys marked "(titles only)" were known from the table of contents of that index, not read page by page. The GitHub Classroom pages were still online although the service was retired on 2026-08-28 (CL-classroom).

Decisions taken for this domain (criteria in order: zero cost, the services' terms, security, simplicity, CLAUDE.md): (1) OSCR has no plans, prices, seats, licences, trials, payments, coupons, invoices or taxes: every feature is free for every account, so the billing surface is excluded; only its information survives, as a per-account and per-lab usage page (12) and a public "Limits" page (16) showing use of OSCR's fixed free quotas, with in-site notices at 90% and 100% (01), never by email. (2) There is no enterprise tier, identity provider, SAML, SCIM, managed users, IP allow list or data-residency choice, as the Authentication and Organizations sections already decided. An institution appears through its ROR-keyed institution page, which also lists the labs that declared that ROR id, read only and with no power over them. The enterprise governance features that cost nothing are already given to every lab (rulesets, repository policies, custom roles and properties, audit log and its API, banner, exports). (3) Enterprise incident response becomes two operator tools for the platform owner (16): a read-only mode set as a Worker variable, and bulk revocation of token rows (hashes only, no secret handled). (4) Audit log streaming becomes an `audit` webhook event and a pull feed (10), never a connector to a paid sink. (5) GitHub Education benefits are excluded: there is nothing to unlock, and enrolment documents and academic emails are personal data OSCR must not collect. GitHub retired Classroom on 2026-08-28; its course administration is excluded, and two ideas are adapted to research: the feedback pull request becomes a whole-repository review for journal code review and artifact evaluation (04), and assignments become reproduction exercises (a lab project of papers, the participants' forks and their reproduction reports; no grading, no roster, no code run; 06). The Community Exchange becomes two discovery listings, "Seeking collaborators" and "Teaching and reproduction material" (08). (6) No money flows through OSCR: Marketplace sales and GitHub Sponsors payments are excluded; the integrations directory stays free and funding appears as links and grants.

## 5. Changelog

Every entry of github.blog/changelog from 2025-10-01 to 2026-09-29, by quarter.

### 5.1 Changelog 2025-10 to 2025-12

*File `data/night/parity/50-changelog-2025-10.md`: 133 rows (Reproduce 27, Adapt 23, Exclude 83).*

Sources read (2026-09-28): every entry of the GitHub changelog dated 2025-10-01 to 2025-12-31, month by month: [October](https://github.blog/changelog/2025/10/) (63 entries), [November](https://github.blog/changelog/2025/11/) (55) and [December](https://github.blog/changelog/2025/12/) (58). That makes 176 entries. Their full text was read through the blog's public WordPress API (`/wp-json/wp/v2/changelogs`, which gives the same total of 176). One entry is left out on purpose: the upcoming deprecation of CodeQL Action v3 (2025-10-28), a version change that removes no feature.

Decisions taken here (criteria in order: zero cost, the services' terms, security, simplicity, CLAUDE.md):
1. About half the period is Copilot: models, agents, the CLI, IDE features and their administration. These entries are excluded, as decided in the Copilot section: no generative model on request, no coding agent, no code execution. OSCR keeps only the purpose of a feature, never its model: rule-based change groups in a pull request, plain default commit messages, Collections in place of Spaces, and `oscr mcp` in place of the MCP server.
2. Enterprise-only entries (Enterprise Cloud and Enterprise Server, data residency, enterprise teams, AI controls, Copilot metrics) and billing entries get one row each, marked Exclude. OSCR has no enterprise tier and no billing. Labs get teams, roles and rulesets in phase 09.
3. Actions, runner and CodeQL entries are excluded because OSCR runs nothing. Their results reach OSCR from a researcher's GitHub mirror: SARIF uploads and statuses posted with GitHub OIDC tokens (phase 10). The new `check_run_id` claim is recorded so that each result links to the exact job.
4. New here: OSCR's personal tokens follow the hardening npm applied in late 2025. There is no unscoped token, a write token expires within 90 days, and tokens are managed from the command line (`oscr token`).
5. New here: `oscr mcp` cleans every user-written text before a model reads it (invisible Unicode, hidden HTML, unrendered Markdown). It also has a lockdown mode that returns only content from a repository's writers and from verified authors of the linked papers.
6. Dependency ecosystems are adapted only where their files can be read as text: uv, Julia, Conda and Go. Bazel and OpenTofu are excluded because updating their lockfiles means running their tools. No secret needs to be created for this section.

### 5.2 Changelog 2026-01 to 2026-03

*File `data/night/parity/51-changelog-2026-01.md`: 81 rows (Reproduce 28, Adapt 34, Exclude 19).*

Sources read (2026-09-28): every entry of [github.blog/changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/) dated 2026-01-01 to 2026-03-31, month by month: 193 entries (38 in January, 72 in February, 83 in March), listed from the archive pages [2026/01](https://github.blog/changelog/2026/01/), [2026/02](https://github.blog/changelog/2026/02/), [2026/03](https://github.blog/changelog/2026/03/) and read in full through the blog's public WordPress API; the two listings match entry for entry. Every entry appears in at least one row. Copilot, Actions runner, CodeQL, enterprise-only and billing entries are grouped, one row each, and excluded for the reasons already decided in the Copilot, Actions, code-security and organizations sections.

| Feature | What it does | Decision | In OSCR (how, or why not) | Phase | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Move work to an organization (replaces turning a user account into an organization) | The direct conversion of a personal account into an organization is removed; a "Move work" flow transfers the selected repositories to a new or existing organization and keeps the personal account | Adapt | No account-to-organization conversion at all: an OSCR account is a person signed in with ORCID, GitHub or Google, and stays a person. A "Move repositories to a lab" step transfers several repositories at once with the ordinary transfer rules (redirects, stars, issues, pull requests). Research: a lab gathers a former student's repositories; DOI links, Zenodo records and tracing maps (pinned to commits, which do not change) keep working through the redirects | 09 | [CL 2026-01-12](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-01-12-deprecation-of-user-to-organization-account-transformation) |

### 5.3 Changelog 2026-04 to 2026-06

*File `data/night/parity/52-changelog-2026-04.md`: 90 rows (Reproduce 25, Adapt 42, Exclude 23).*

Sources read (2026-09-28): all 260 entries of https://github.blog/changelog/ dated 2026-04-01 to 2026-06-30 (85 in April, 68 in May, 107 in June), each read in full through the changelog's public listing (`/wp-json/wp/v2/changelogs`). Every entry is in at least one row. AI products, enterprise-only items and billing items are grouped into one row each theme, marked Exclude.

| Feature | What it does | Decision | In OSCR (how, or why not) | Phase | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Improved issue search: semantic and hybrid, best-match sort, `search_type` in the API | Natural-language search over issue titles and bodies, combined with keyword matching; results sorted by relevance; REST `search_type=semantic` or `hybrid` and GraphQL `searchType`, 10 queries a minute | Adapt | Issue search runs on D1 FTS5 (BM25) over titles and bodies, sorted by best match by default, with phrases and filters; it runs only when the form is submitted (CLAUDE.md). No embeddings: hosted inference is not free, and the local model's GPU window (01:00 to 07:00) cannot answer live queries. The public API takes the same query string. ### 5.4 Changelog 2026-07 to 2026-09

*File `data/night/parity/53-changelog-2026-07.md`: 214 rows (Reproduce 50, Adapt 44, Exclude 120).*

Sources read (2026-09-28): every entry of the GitHub changelog (https://github.blog/changelog/) dated 2026-07-01 to 2026-09-29, read in full, month by month, through the changelog's own feed (`https://github.blog/wp-json/wp/v2/changelogs`, the data behind the page): 240 entries, 92 in July, 70 in August and 78 in September (the latest is dated 2026-09-25). Every entry is cited in at least one row. For consistency: `docs/NIGHT_RUN.md`, `docs/ACCOUNTS.md` and the sections already in `data/night/parity/`. Below, "section NN" is the file NN of that folder; a bare number in brackets is a night phase.

Decisions taken here (criteria in order: zero cost, the services' terms, security, simplicity, CLAUDE.md):
1. **Copilot, models and agents are excluded**, as in section 16: no generative model runs on request, and no agent runs code. When a Copilot feature serves a purpose OSCR needs, OSCR keeps the purpose and drops the model: the repository overview is built from metadata, review guidelines come from a file, suggestion controls apply to the Mac's rules and night model, and custom property values come from templates.
2. **Enterprise-only and billing items get one row each, marked Exclude.** An item announced twice (preview then general availability, or a notice then the removal) has one row with both entries.
3. **Repetitive families are grouped**, each row citing every entry: new models, model retirements, CodeQL releases, hosted runner images, and the Copilot roundups (VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains, Mobile, weekly).
4. **npm's supply-chain measures are adopted for research code:** a dual-use DISCLOSURE file (16), a "draft only" release permission for CI (07), several trusted OIDC configurations per repository (10), publication only after the malware check (07), a 72-hour hold on sensitive writes after an account recovery (NEW: Account security), and no token that can manage the account (01).
5. **Redirect URIs of OSCR applications are matched exactly**; wildcard matching is excluded. For "À valider par Yann": GitHub now shows, and has turned on by legacy, wildcard redirect matching for every OAuth app with a single redirect URI. OSCR's two GitHub sign-in OAuth apps (production and local development, one callback each, `docs/ACCOUNTS.md`) are in that case. The owner switches the option off in each app's settings on GitHub. No secret is involved.
6. **Moderation never limits, closes or prunes research reports.** Section 12's rule is extended to the new tools: the triage restriction on issue creation, pull request limits, blocking from a comment, "close all contributions" and the edit-history cap never apply to code-error, code–paper mismatch or reproduction-failure reports.
7. **New phases proposed:** "Automated-decision transparency" (as in section 16), "Account security" (as in section 04), and "Service status and help".

## 6. Addenda from the completeness critics

Features the critics found missing, each checked on its documentation page. The first column names the domain of section 4 the feature belongs to.

### 6.1 Addendum 1.1: features found by the completeness critics

*File `data/night/parity/910-addendum.md`: 19 rows (Reproduce 0, Adapt 10, Exclude 9).*

Sources read (2026-09-28): the fifteen pages the critics named (column Source), plus [special-events](https://docs.github.com/en/enterprise-server@3.19/support/learning-about-github-support/about-github-special-events-support) (Special Events Support has its own page, not a section of the Premium page), [subtree](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/using-git/about-git-subtree-merges) (the subtree merge page, separate from the split page) and [personalize](https://docs.github.com/en/account-and-profile/tutorials/personalize-your-profile).

Verification: all fifteen exist, so none was skipped. Three overlap rows already in the inventory. Each is kept here only for what it adds:
- the matrix adds to "Tested environments" (14-actions);
- the Company field adds to the affiliation of the "Location" row (02-account);
- the nonprofit discounts are covered by "Discounted plans" (27-out-of-scope-areas).

The REST API documents the profile's `company` field. The docs do not describe the `@org` link inside it: that behaviour comes from the settings form's hint. The Dependabot page says that Dependabot-triggered runs use Dependabot secrets, not Actions secrets. It does not show the read-only token rule, so this table does not rely on it.

Decisions taken here (criteria in order: zero cost, the services' terms, security, simplicity, CLAUDE.md):
1. Nothing that needs a workflow to run is built. What it automates becomes non-executing features or a display of the mirror's results.
2. The "support" features become a ticket in the site: no email, no attachment other than text, no response-time promise, no AI assistant.
3. The two Git workflows (split, subtree) work unchanged over OSCR's HTTPS Git. OSCR adds provenance relations that it verifies from the pushed objects, as data, so that tracing maps survive a split or an inclusion.
4. Maintenance mode is taken from the Enterprise Server administration, which is otherwise excluded, as a read-only switch for OSCR's own migrations.

| actions | Matrix strategy (running variations of a job) | `strategy.matrix` expands one job into one job per combination of variables (for example OS × Python version). `include` adds or augments combinations and `exclude` removes some. `fail-fast` cancels the others when one fails, `max-parallel` caps concurrent jobs and `continue-on-error` can depend on the matrix. A matrix can be built at run time from a context or from `fromJSON` of a job output. At most 256 jobs | Adapt | OSCR runs nothing, so it never expands a matrix into jobs, and it shows `fail-fast`, `max-parallel` and `continue-on-error` as read, without applying them. The Mac reads the mirror's workflow files as data, with a safe YAML loader, and expands `matrix` with GitHub's documented `include`/`exclude` rules, capped at 256 combinations. The result is an **environment grid** on the repository's Checks tab and on the paper's Code section, with one cell per combination. Each cell holds the mirror's job conclusion for that commit, matched by the job's name (`test (ubuntu-latest, 3.11)`) and read with the read-only token `org.oscr.github`. It also holds the reproduction reports (05) filed against that environment. A matrix built at run time cannot be expanded statically: it shows "computed at run time", with a link to the run. Research: a reader sees which OS and language versions the code cited by a paper was tested on, and where a reproduction failed. This extends "Tested environments" in 14-actions | 10 | https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-what-workflows-do/run-job-variations |

It reads this from the pushed objects and executes nothing. The file tree and the repository page show it, with that code's papers and license. The license compatibility check (11) compares the two licenses. Tracing maps of the included repository resolve in the including one through the prefix. The usual case is an analysis repository that includes a published toolbox at the version its paper cites | 01 | https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/using-git/about-git-subtree-merges |

The settings form's hint says that `@org` in it links the organization | Adapt | The profile already has a structured affiliation linked to the ROR institution pages ("Location" row, 02-account).
