It is filled by the person, or proposed at sign-in from their public ORCID employment record. It is never taken from the private `contact` table, whose affiliations go only to the private dataset (CLAUDE.md). An email-like string is refused, as in the bio | 08 | https://docs.github.com/en/rest/users/users#update-the-authenticated-user |

### 6.2 Addendum 1.2: features found by the completeness critics

*File `data/night/parity/911-addendum.md`: 4 rows (Reproduce 1, Adapt 3, Exclude 0).*

Sources read (2026-09-28): [rest/commits/comments](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/commits/comments), [rest/guides/working-with-comments](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/guides/working-with-comments), [rest/pulls/pulls](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/pulls/pulls), [rest/commits/commits](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/commits/commits), [cli/cli#8755](https://github.com/cli/cli/issues/8755), [community discussion 61107](https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/61107) and the page [managing-a-branch-protection-rule](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-protected-branches/managing-a-branch-protection-rule). All four features exist. The inventory had only the commit-comment switch (05, 12, 18, 51) and the `diff`/`patch` API media types (19). The row "Description, website, topics" (05) mentions the sidebar sections only in passing, and nothing covered the Danger Zone switch. None of the four duplicates an existing row, so none is skipped.

| Domain | Feature | What it does | Decision | In OSCR (how, or why not) | Phase | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| repos-files | Comment on a commit (commit comments) | On a commit page, anyone who can read the repository comments on the whole commit or on one line of its diff, outside any pull request. The REST API lists, gets, creates, edits and deletes these comments: `body`, optional `path` and `position` (diff index; `line` is deprecated). Creating one sends notifications, reactions are counted, and creating comments too fast hits secondary rate limits. | Reproduce | Built on Phase 04's line-comment model, anchored to (commit, path, side, line), and shown on the commit page of 02. The API also accepts GitHub's `position`, which the commit's precomputed diff converts to a file line. Signed-in accounts only, with Turnstile and a per-account daily limit (16). Notifications are in the site only, never by email. Every address in a comment body is masked (`catalog.mask_emails`). Rows go in D1 `oscr_community`. The repository switch that turns commit comments off (05, 12, 18) still applies. On a mirrored repository, comments stay on OSCR: nothing is posted to GitHub, because OSCR never stores a provider's token. Research: when a comment is on a commit that a paper, a release or a validated tracing map cites, the paper's page says so in words ("2 comments on the cited commit"). A line comment on a mapped line shows its Methods paragraph (in full under an open licence, otherwise a summary and a link, decision D1). A comment can be turned into a "code-paper mismatch" or "code error" issue (05). The commit and its links stay unchanged. | 04 (shown on 02's commit page; API in 10) | [rest/commits/comments](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/commits/comments), [working-with-comments](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/guides/working-with-comments) |
| pull-requests | `.diff` and `.patch` URLs for pull requests, commits and comparisons | Adding `.diff` or `.patch` to a pull request, commit or compare URL returns the plain-text diff or the `git format-patch` mailbox, ready for `git apply` or `git am`. The API exposes them as `diff_url` and `patch_url` (pull request and compare objects) and as the `diff`/`patch` media types. Large diffs may time out. | Adapt | Same URL forms: `/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<sha>.diff\|.patch`, `/pull/<n>.diff\|.patch` (the three-dot diff; the patch is the series of the head's commits) and `/compare/<a>...<b>.diff\|.patch`. `diff_url` and `patch_url` appear in the API (10), and `oscr pr diff --patch` in the command-line tool (14). Changes for OSCR: (1) the `GitBackend` builds the files with read-only Git commands (`git diff`, `git format-patch --stdout`), precomputed at push for commits and at each push to a pull request's head. Comparisons are built once per (base SHA, head SHA) and cached. The Worker only streams the stored file (10 ms of CPU), and no user code ever runs. (2) No email is ever shown (CLAUDE.md): the `From:` header gets a no-reply address built from the account handle (or from a hash for authors without an account), and `Signed-off-by:` and `Co-authored-by:` trailers and addresses in messages are masked. A help page explains that `git am` then records the no-reply address. (3) The files are served as `text/plain; charset=utf-8` with `nosniff` (no HTML from the site's origin), and URLs addressed by SHA get immutable cache headers. (4) Past the diff limits of 08 ("Diff and listing limits"), a plain-text notice gives the `git fetch` and `git format-patch` commands instead. Research: "Changes since the paper's version" (06, "File history") gets a `.diff` link, so a reader sees in plain text what changed after the published results. A reproduction report (05) cites the exact `.patch`, at fixed SHAs, of the fix it needed. | 02 (04 for pull requests) | [rest/pulls/pulls](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/pulls/pulls), [rest/commits/commits](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/commits/commits) |
| repos-manage | "Include in the home page" toggles for Releases, Packages and Deployments | Checkboxes in the About panel's gear dialog show or hide the Releases, Packages and Deployments sections of the repository sidebar. GitHub has no API for them (the `gh` request is open and blocked). | Adapt | This refines row "Description, website, topics" (05). OSCR's sidebar has two optional sections: Releases (07) and Environment and packages (the package and container records of "NEW: Environments and packages", 15). Each has a toggle in the About dialog, shown by default and stored as a boolean on the repository's D1 row. Unlike GitHub, OSCR also exposes the toggles in the API (10) and in `oscr repo edit` (14). Deployments has no counterpart, because OSCR hosts no deployments (15, 19). Research: the sections that tie the code to science cannot be hidden: linked papers and their DOIs, "Cite this repository", tracing maps and reproduction reports. The code-paper link is the registry's purpose, the same reason a linked repository cannot turn private (05, "Change visibility"). | 02 | [cli/cli#8755](https://github.com/cli/cli/issues/8755) |
| repos-manage | Disable branch protection rules (Danger Zone) | A Danger Zone switch in the repository settings turns off, at once, the enforcement of every classic branch protection rule and the protection APIs. An admin turns them back on from the same place (GitHub staff, community discussion 61107). The docs page on branch protection rules does not describe it. | Adapt | OSCR has no classic rules, only rulesets (05, "Classic branch protection rules"), and each ruleset already has the Active, Evaluate and Disabled states (18). The switch becomes "Suspend this repository's rulesets" in the repository's Danger zone. It is for admins only, asks the admin to type the repository name and give a reason, sets every repository-level ruleset to Disabled and remembers each ruleset's earlier state. "Resume" restores those states. Lab (organization) rulesets are untouched. Rulesets are public, so a silent switch would mislead readers about how the code is protected. The suspension is therefore stated in words on the public `/rules` page ("suspended on \<date> by \<handle>: \<reason>") and written to the audit log (09), and the admins get an in-site reminder every 7 days while it lasts. It never lifts OSCR's own safeguards, which are not rulesets: the push gate's size, secret and malware checks (01, 11, 16) stay on. Research: commits pinned by a paper, a release or a validated tracing map stay reachable even through force pushes (05, "Block force pushes"). | 09 | [community discussion 61107](https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/61107) |

All twelve features exist. Two are skipped because an existing row already names and decides them:

- **`gh extension exec`**: the "Extensions: model" row of `20-cli-desktop-mobile.md` names it and cites its manual page. Clarification of that row: OSCR needs no `exec` subcommand, because an `oscr-<name>` program is on the `PATH` and can be run directly when a core command has the same name (Git's model).

The other ten follow. The expansion of web diffs was decided only indirectly, by the GitHub Desktop row "Expand diff context" ("Same (02)"). The row below states it for OSCR's own diffs.

| Domain | Feature | What it does | Decision | In OSCR (how, or why not) | Phase | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| pull-requests | Expand unchanged lines in web diffs (unfold context) | In every diff GitHub renders (a pull request's Files changed, a commit, a comparison), unfold buttons in the gutter show more unchanged lines above or below a hunk, one step at a time or up to the whole file. OSCR's step is 20 lines per click, plus "Expand all" for the whole file. The button fetches the file at the diff's right-hand commit once. That file is addressed by its SHA, so it never changes and the browser caches it. The lines are then inserted in the page: no model, no build, nothing run. The limits of "Diff and listing limits" (08) still apply: past 500 KB per file, the button gives the `git show <sha>:<path>` command instead. The buttons are real `button` elements with a label ("Show 20 lines above line 120"), usable from the keyboard and read by screen readers (15). Their look is a rule added to `science.css`. A reviewer can comment on an expanded line like on any other line (04, "comment on unchanged lines"). Research: an expanded line that a tracing map links says so in words ("linked to Methods, paragraph 3") with a link to the Code ↔ Paper reader at that commit. From such a line, a reviewer can open a "code-paper mismatch" issue (05). | 02 (review in 04) | [expanding context in diffs](https://github.blog/2013-12-02-expanding-context-in-diffs/) |
| repos-manage | Partial (blobless or treeless) and shallow clones | The Git server supports partial clone (`--filter=blob:none`, `--filter=tree:0`) and shallow clone (`--depth=N`). A large repository (big data files, long history) is fetched without every blob or every commit, and missing objects come when a command needs them. It combines with sparse-checkout. Shallow clones make `git log` and `merge-base` unreliable and later fetches expensive. Treeless clones make file history expensive. | Reproduce | This is a property of the Git server, so it depends on the `GitBackend`. (1) With the user-owned GitHub backend (the storage reports' recommended primary, U1), the server is GitHub: every form works as is. (2) `GitBackend` gets capability flags (`partial_clone`, `shallow`, `protocol_v2`). A backend added later must advertise them before it can host large repositories. Cloudflare Artifacts, for example, does not support `filter` (`data/night/storage/cloudflare.md`, §4.1). (3) The clone box (01, "Code button") and the "Quick setup" page offer "without the full history" (blobless) next to the plain URL. A help page ("Clone a large research repository") says when to use each form: blobless for working on the code, shallow only for a one-off run, treeless for CI. It warns that `blame` and history are incomplete in a shallow clone, and it advises recording the full commit SHA in a reproduction report. (4) The Mac already reads repositories this way (`oscr/repos.py`: `git clone --filter=blob:none --depth 1 --no-checkout`, then `git show` for the licence and README only). (2) `oscr-checks-config-file` (text) names a file in the repository that can add rules or exclude paths from the extra packs. (3) `oscr-checks-coverage-on-prs` (true/false) shows, on a pull request, which files each check read. `disable-overlay` has no counterpart: there is no incremental analysis to turn off. No property can lower the baseline: secret refusal at push, malware blocking and the licence check always run (NIGHT_RUN rule 8). On a GitHub mirror, GitHub's own `github-codeql-*` properties act on the GitHub side, and OSCR only shows the SARIF it receives (11). | actions | Container customization hooks for self-hosted runners | `ACTIONS_RUNNER_CONTAINER_HOOKS` gives the absolute path of a script that replaces how a Linux self-hosted runner creates job and service containers. All six features exist. Three are skipped because an existing row already names and decides them:

- **Job start and end hooks on self-hosted runners** (`ACTIONS_RUNNER_HOOK_JOB_STARTED`, `ACTIONS_RUNNER_HOOK_JOB_COMPLETED`): the "Self-hosted runners" row of `14-actions.md` lists the pre- and post-job scripts and excludes them, because OSCR runs no job and no runner. - **Copy the default branch only when forking**: the "Fork a repository" row of `08-pull-requests.md` reproduces the form with its "Copy the DEFAULT branch only" checkbox, and the `gh repo fork` row of `20-cli-desktop-mobile.md` reproduces `--default-branch-only` in `oscr repo fork`. One part of that page has no row yet: copying an upstream branch into the fork later, from the fork's Branches page. The last row below covers it.
- **Include all branches when creating from a template**: the "Create from a template" row of `05-repos-manage.md` reproduces "default branch only or Include all branches", the "From a template" row of `20-cli-desktop-mobile.md` reproduces `--include-all-branches`, and the Classroom row of `27-out-of-scope-areas.md` points to them. The page adds one detail, which that row's "unrelated history" already implies: the copied branches have unrelated histories, so no pull request or merge is possible between them. OSCR's comparison page will say so in words ("no common history") instead of showing an empty diff.

The Slack and Teams channel subscriptions and reminders are already decided in `03-notifications.md`: Adapt, through webhooks (10) and the in-site "Waiting for your review" digest. The two chat rows below cover what those rows leave out: actions taken from the chat, and previews of links.

### 6.5 Addendum 4.1: features found by the completeness critics

*File `data/night/parity/940-addendum.md`: 6 rows (Reproduce 1, Adapt 2, Exclude 3).*

Sources read (2026-09-28): [ask-a-side-question](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/use-copilot-cli/ask-a-side-question), [steer-agents](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/use-copilot-cli/steer-agents), [context-management](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/copilot-cli/context-management), [utility-models](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/models/utility-models), [fedramp-models](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/enterprise/fedramp-models), [open-with-deep-links](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/github-copilot-app/open-with-deep-links), the Actions toolkit's [problem-matchers.md](https://github.com/actions/toolkit/blob/main/docs/problem-matchers.md), [editorconfig.org](https://editorconfig.org/) and [ignoring-files](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/git-basics/ignoring-files). That last page no longer mentions GitHub Desktop, so Desktop's ignore commands were checked in two Git lessons for GitHub Desktop, [Caltech Library, "Ignoring Things"](https://software.library.caltech.edu/git-desktop/05-ignore/) (Repository settings > Ignored Files) and [McMaster, "Ignoring Things"](https://jcszamosi.github.io/mcmaster_swc_git_gui/04-ignore/) (right-click "Ignore" or "Ignore all .dat files"), and in Desktop's issue [#11749](https://github.com/desktop/desktop/issues/11749) (the menu label "Ignore File (add to .gitignore)"). On OSCR's side: the decisions and CLI rows of `16-copilot.md`, the decisions, "Workflow commands and annotations" and "Reproduction check" rows of `14-actions.md`, the tab-size rows of `02-account.md`, `06-repos-files.md` and `24-ux.md`, the Desktop rows of `20-cli-desktop-mobile.md` ("Diff tab size" included), the editor and upload rows of `06-repos-files.md`, and the free-tier table of `docs/PLATFORM_PLAN.md` §2.

All nine features exist. Three are skipped because an existing row already names and decides them:

- **Context management and compaction in Copilot CLI** (`/compact`, `/context`, session checkpoints): the "CLI sessions" row of `16-copilot.md` names `/context`, `/compact` and automatic compaction and excludes them (no agent). The checkpoints (`/session checkpoints`, one saved summary per compaction) belong to the same excluded sessions. One fact in that row needs a correction: compaction starts at about 80% of the context window, not 95%; at about 95% the CLI pauses until the compaction ends. The decision does not change.
- **FedRAMP Moderate model policy**: the "Enterprise governance" row of `16-copilot.md` names "FedRAMP models" and excludes them (no model). The page adds what makes it doubly out of scope: an enterprise policy (GitHub Enterprise Cloud with US data residency) that limits members to nine certified models and costs 10% more AI credits.
- **Deep links to the GitHub Copilot app** (`ghapp://`, wrapped in `https://github.com/copilot/app/launch?open=`): the "GitHub Copilot app" row of `16-copilot.md` names the deep links and excludes the app (agents). The links OSCR does build already open a free tool at a precise place: the `vscode://vscode.git/clone?url=` link and "clone the version cited by the paper" in the clone menu (02), and the `codespaces.new` link for a GitHub mirror (`15-packages-pages-codespaces.md`). The page's own warning, never to put secrets or sensitive content in a link, matches OSCR's rule that no personal data goes into a URL; OSCR's prefilled new-issue links carry only a title, a body, a DOI, a commit, a path and lines (05).

Decisions taken here (criteria in order: zero cost, the services' terms, security, simplicity, CLAUDE.md): (1) the three remaining Copilot features are excluded for the reasons of `16-copilot.md`: no generative model runs on request, and there is no agent; (2) **no regular expression written by a user runs on OSCR's side**. Problem matchers are applied by `oscr` on the researcher's own machine, to the log of a run the researcher made there, and OSCR receives only the matches, checked as data; (3) **EditorConfig is read as data when the Mac processes a push**, never parsed per request, and the reader's own tab-size choice wins over the repository's; (4) **Desktop's ignore commands become three commits made on the site**, through the web editor's commit dialog, with the rules of protected branches.

| Domain | Feature | What it does | Decision | In OSCR (how, or why not) | Phase | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| copilot | Side question in Copilot CLI (`/ask`, alias `/btw`) | In a local interactive session, `/ask <question>` gets an answer in a dialog separate from the main conversation. The model uses the current conversation as context but cannot use tools, and neither the question nor the answer enters the history. Esc cancels or dismisses the dialog; a follow-up needs a new `/ask`. Not available in remote sessions. | Exclude | It is a question to a hosted model inside an agent session. OSCR runs no generative model on request and no agent (decisions 1 and 2 of `16-copilot.md`), so there is no conversation to step aside from, and the `oscr` tool (14) contains no model. Nothing is lost for research: a question about a paper's code is asked in the open, in the repository's Discussions or on the paper's page (06), where the authors' answer also helps the next reader. |, | [ask-a-side-question](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/use-copilot-cli/ask-a-side-question) |
| copilot | Steering and message queueing in Copilot CLI | While the agent works, a plain prompt (Enter) steers the running task at once: stop it going the wrong way, or narrow its scope. Ctrl+Enter or Ctrl+Q queues the message instead: it waits for the current task to end and runs as the next turn. | Exclude | No agent, so nothing to steer or queue. Steering is already excluded in `16-copilot.md` ("Session control" for the cloud agent, "Remote control and cloud sessions" for the CLI); queueing is the part no row named, and it is excluded for the same reason. They use no premium requests or tokens, but they have per-user rate limits. | Exclude | No hosted model, and none that a user cannot turn off. What they do already has a counterpart without a model: the web editor proposes a plain default commit message ("Update `<path>`", 03; `16-copilot.md` "Commit messages and conflict help in GitHub Desktop"), and there are no chat sessions to title. OSCR's only model is the local one on the Mac, used for classification between 01:00 and 07:00 (CLAUDE.md), and every value it sets is labelled "set by the model" with its confidence (the "Automated-decision transparency" phase proposed in `16-copilot.md`): the opposite of a model working unseen in the background. |, | [utility-models](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/models/utility-models) |
| actions | Problem matchers (`::add-matcher::`, `::remove-matcher owner=…::`) | A step registers a JSON file: an `owner` id, a default `severity`, and a `pattern` array of regular expressions whose groups give `file`, `line`, `column`, `severity`, `code`, `message` and `fromPath`. A matcher is single-line, or multi-line with consecutive patterns (`loop` on the last one repeats it). Each match in the step's log becomes an annotation at the file and line, and the log line is decorated. Limits: 10 errors, 10 warnings and 10 notices per step, 50 per job. `::remove-matcher owner=…::` turns one off. Separate from writing `::error::` yourself. | Adapt | OSCR runs no job, so it has no log of its own to scan. And it never runs a regular expression taken from a repository: run in the Worker (10 ms of CPU per request) or on the Mac, a badly written one can backtrack without end. The result reaches OSCR by two paths. (1) **Mirrors**: on GitHub, matcher annotations are check-run annotations, so they arrive with the check runs the Mac imports (`14-actions.md` "Workflow commands and annotations") and are shown at the lines of the commit, within the 200 annotations per check run. The decorated log stays on GitHub, behind the "open on GitHub" link. (2) **Reproductions**: `oscr repro report --log run.log` (14) applies matchers on the researcher's own machine, to the log of a run the researcher made there. It uses the repository's own matcher files (same JSON format, read from `.github/` or `.oscr/matchers/`) and built-in matchers for research toolchains: Python tracebacks, R's "Error in", MATLAB's "Error in … (line N)", Julia stack frames, gcc and gfortran messages. Local paths are cut to paths inside the repository (`fromPath`), and messages go through `catalog.mask_emails`. Only the matches are sent, never the log. On receipt, OSCR checks each match (the path exists at the reported commit, the line is inside the file, at most 10 per level and 50 per report) and attaches the matches to the `repro/…` check (`14-actions.md` "Reproduction check"). Research link: a failure at a line covered by a tracing map is also listed under that Methods paragraph ("the reproduction failed at `train.py` line 112, which the map links to paragraph 3"). The "Open a reproduction-failure issue" form (05) is prefilled with those lines at that commit. | 10, 14 | [problem-matchers.md](https://github.com/actions/toolkit/blob/main/docs/problem-matchers.md) |
| repos-files | EditorConfig in the code viewer and the web editor (refinement of "Tab size preference" and "Diff tab size") | GitHub reads a repository's `.editorconfig` files. For each file, the sections whose glob matches it set `indent_style`, `indent_size` and `tab_width`, which give the width of tabs in the file view and the indentation in the browser editor. The specification: the files are searched upward from the file's folder, the closest one wins, and `root = true` stops the search. Its other properties are `end_of_line`, `charset`, `trim_trailing_whitespace` and `insert_final_newline`. editorconfig.org lists "GitHub (code viewer and editor)" among the tools that need no plugin. | Reproduce | **Reading**: when the Mac processes a push (the job that runs OSCR's checks, which read the tree as data), it reads every `.editorconfig` of the commit, each at most 64 KiB, with globs translated in bounded time (no backtracking). It resolves `indent_style`, `indent_size` and `tab_width` for each file; the search stops at the repository's root. The result is stored with the commit's file metadata, so neither the Worker nor the browser parses anything. **Viewer (02)**: static pages carry the width, written at build time, as a `data-tab-size` attribute on `ol.lines` (1 to 8; wider values are shown as 8), with the matching rules added to `science.css`; pages rendered on demand read the same stored number. Precedence: the reader's own tab-size choice (`02-account.md`, `24-ux.md`) when they made one, otherwise the repository's `.editorconfig`, otherwise 8, as in Git. The file's header says which one applies, in words ("tabs shown as 4 columns, from .editorconfig"). **Editor (03)**: CodeMirror 6 follows `indent_style`, `indent_size` and `tab_width`. `end_of_line` applies to files created in the editor; existing files keep their line endings (`06-repos-files.md`). `trim_trailing_whitespace` and `insert_final_newline` touch only the lines the session changed, so saving never rewrites lines nobody edited. A file whose `charset` is not UTF-8 opens read only, and the page gives the reason (the editor saves UTF-8). Research link: the Code ↔ Paper reader's code pane and permalinked line ranges (snippets, 13) use the same width, so a mapped range reads as the authors wrote it.
